segments.title: HMS Foxglove's three-decade Acacia-class career
segments.summary: HMS Foxglove was an Acacia-class Royal Navy minesweeper launched in 1915 and kept in service until 1946.
segments.body: HMS Foxglove was an Acacia-class Royal Navy minesweeper, launched by Barclay Curle in Glasgow and commissioned in 1915. Minesweeping was the class's primary purpose, assigning this small sloop a specialized and dangerous job. Foxglove was not scrapped until 1946, after a service life that spanned both world wars. Her career shows how long the Royal Navy could keep a modest specialist vessel useful.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies Foxglove as an Acacia-class Royal Navy minesweeper, gives her 1915 launch and commission, and notes her 1946 scrapping.

segments.title: Foxglove's compact hull and proportions
segments.summary: Foxglove displaced about 1,200 tons, with a reported length between 250 and 262 feet 6 inches, a 33-foot beam, and a 12-foot draft.
segments.body: Foxglove displaced roughly 1,200 tons. Her reported length varies with the measurement used, from about 250 feet to 262 feet 6 inches, while her beam was 33 feet and her draft about 12 feet. Both the bow and stern are described as not very pronounced. Together, these figures show the compact scale and shape of a vessel built primarily for minesweeping.

evidence.note: The transcript gives Foxglove's approximate displacement, alternative length measurements, beam, draft, and the limited projection of her bow and stern.

segments.title: Foxglove's armament changed during service
segments.summary: The Acacia-class design specified two 12-pounders and two 3-pounders, while Foxglove's reported service fits included 4-inch guns and additional 3-pounders.
segments.body: The Acacia-class design called for two 12-pounder guns and two 3-pounders. Foxglove did not necessarily carry that nominal battery throughout her career. At several points she appears to have been fitted with 4-inch guns and additional 3-pounders. The comparison separates a class design's paper armament from the weapons carried by an individual ship at different times.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Foxglove's designed 12-pounder and 3-pounder armament with reported four-inch-gun fits and additional 3-pounders.

segments.title: From World War I minesweeping to wider wartime service
segments.summary: Foxglove spent about two years sweeping mines before moving into broader fighting duties in 1917.
segments.body: Foxglove's early World War I work was primarily minesweeping, the dangerous specialist task for which the Acacia class had been built. She spent about two years in that role before the Royal Navy redirected her in 1917. Her later duties are described only as broader war-fighting work, without a named operation. The reassignment shows how wartime demand could pull a purpose-built minesweeper into general naval service.

evidence.note: The transcript says Foxglove performed minesweeping duties until 1917 before being turned to broader war-fighting work.

segments.title: China Station rescue work with HMS Carlisle
segments.summary: On the China Station, Foxglove helped HMS Carlisle rescue survivors from the grounded SS Hong Moh in 1921.
segments.body: During her 1920s China Station service, Foxglove responded after SS Hong Moh grounded near White Rock off Lamock Island on 3 March 1921. She and the C-class cruiser HMS Carlisle assisted the passengers. Together, the two Royal Navy ships rescued 221 survivors. The incident shows the maritime rescue work that could fall to ships serving on a distant station.

evidence.note: The transcript places Foxglove on the China Station and describes the 3 March 1921 rescue effort with HMS Carlisle, including 221 survivors.

segments.title: Dive-bomb damage and wartime support service
segments.summary: German dive bombers damaged Foxglove off the Isle of Wight in July 1940, but she remained afloat and served out the war in support roles.
segments.body: German aircraft dive-bombed and damaged Foxglove off the Isle of Wight in July 1940, ending her active wartime contribution early. The ship remained afloat and was converted into an accommodation and base ship. She then served as a harbour guard ship at Londonderry, Northern Ireland, for the rest of the war. The closing career summary also mentions earlier work on the China Station and in the Mediterranean, though it gives no details of her Mediterranean service. Foxglove was scrapped in 1946 after a long career that continued through support duties following the attack.

evidence.note: The transcript describes dive-bomb damage off the Isle of Wight, conversion to accommodation and base-ship roles, harbour guard service at Londonderry, and 1946 scrapping.
The closing remarks mention China Station and Mediterranean service, note that active World War II work ended early in July 1940, and judge the ship a valuable build.
